entry.sum: Interpolation builds the unique polynomial of degree at most $n$ through $n+1$ given data points; numerical integration (quadrature) integrates such a polynomial instead of the original function. The error of both is governed by one formula: the gap $f(x) - p_n(x)$ equals $\frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\prod_i (x - x_i)$, so smooth functions and well-placed nodes give small errors.
key: \int_a^b f\,dx - T_h = -\frac{(b-a)h^2}{12} f''(\xi), \qquad \int_a^b f\,dx - S_h = -\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180} f^{(4)}(\xi)
\text{Gauss rule with } n \text{ nodes is exact for all polynomials of degree} \le 2n-1
entry.why: Almost every integral met in practice, from probabilities under a bell curve to the energy of a vibrating structure, has no closed form and is computed by a quadrature rule; the same polynomial approximations sit inside methods for differential equations and computer graphics.

links.note: Adams multistep methods are obtained by integrating an interpolating polynomial through past slopes, and finite element methods use Gauss quadrature to assemble their matrices.
Expectations such as $E[g(Z)]$ for a normal variable $Z$ are computed with Gauss-Hermite quadrature, which is exact when $g$ is a polynomial of low degree.

refs: Süli & Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
Trefethen, Approximation Theory and Approximation Practice

blocks.body:
You know a function only at a few points: a table of measurements, or a formula so expensive that you can afford to evaluate it a handful of times. How should you guess its values in between, and how should you estimate its integral? The integral $\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx$, for example, has no expression in elementary functions, yet a calculator returns $0.746824\ldots$ instantly. It does so with the ideas on this page.

The plan: replace $f$ by a polynomial that agrees with it at chosen points, and compute with the polynomial. The questions are how large the error is and where to put the points. [[taylor|Taylor's theorem]] matches derivatives at one point; interpolation matches values at several points, and its error formula looks very similar.

blocks.title: Polynomials through given points
blocks.body:
Two points determine a line, three points (with different $x$-coordinates) determine a parabola. In general, given nodes $x_0, \dots, x_n$, all distinct, and values $y_0, \dots, y_n$, we want a polynomial $p$ of degree at most $n$ with $p(x_i) = y_i$ for every $i$.

Lagrange's idea is to build it from pieces that each handle one point. Let
$$\ell_i(x) = \prod_{j \ne i} \frac{x - x_j}{x_i - x_j}.$$
This polynomial has degree $n$, equals $1$ at $x_i$ and $0$ at every other node. Hence
$$p(x) = \sum_{i=0}^{n} y_i\, \ell_i(x)$$
takes the value $y_i$ at $x_i$. For instance, through $(-1, 2)$, $(0, 1)$, $(2, 5)$ we get
$$p(x) = 2\cdot\frac{x(x-2)}{3} + 1\cdot\frac{(x+1)(x-2)}{-2} + 5\cdot\frac{(x+1)x}{6} = x^2 + 1,$$
as you can confirm by expanding.

There can be only one such polynomial. If $p$ and $q$ both work, then $p - q$ has degree at most $n$ and vanishes at $n + 1$ distinct points; a nonzero polynomial of degree at most $n$ has at most $n$ roots, so $p = q$.

Newton's form $p(x) = c_0 + c_1(x - x_0) + c_2(x - x_0)(x - x_1) + \cdots$ describes the same polynomial; its coefficients, the divided differences, come from a triangular table of difference quotients, and adding a node just adds a term.

blocks.title: Interpolation error
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be $n+1$ times differentiable on an interval $[a, b]$ containing the distinct nodes $x_0, \dots, x_n$, and let $p_n$ be the polynomial of degree at most $n$ interpolating $f$ at these nodes. Then for every $x \in [a, b]$ there is $\xi \in (a, b)$, depending on $x$, with
$$f(x) - p_n(x) = \frac{f^{(n+1)}(\xi)}{(n+1)!}\, w(x), \qquad w(x) = \prod_{i=0}^{n} (x - x_i).$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
If $x$ is a node both sides are $0$. Otherwise $w(x) \ne 0$, so we may choose a constant $K$ with $f(x) - p_n(x) = K\,w(x)$. Consider
$$g(t) = f(t) - p_n(t) - K\,w(t).$$
It vanishes at the $n+1$ nodes and at $t = x$: that is $n + 2$ distinct zeros in $[a,b]$. By Rolle's theorem ([[mvt]]) $g'$ has at least $n+1$ zeros between them, $g''$ at least $n$, and so on, until $g^{(n+1)}$ has at least one zero $\xi \in (a,b)$. Now $p_n^{(n+1)} = 0$ because $\deg p_n \le n$, and $w^{(n+1)} = (n+1)!$ because $w$ is monic of degree $n+1$. So $0 = g^{(n+1)}(\xi) = f^{(n+1)}(\xi) - K\,(n+1)!$, which gives $K = f^{(n+1)}(\xi)/(n+1)!$.

blocks.title: Where to put the nodes
blocks.body:
The error formula has two factors. The derivative factor belongs to $f$; the factor $w(x)$ is under our control through the choice of nodes. Equally spaced nodes look natural but are a poor choice for high degree: $|w(x)|$ is much larger near the ends of the interval than in the middle.

Runge's example: interpolate $f(x) = 1/(1 + 25x^2)$ on $[-1, 1]$ at $n + 1$ equally spaced points. With $n = 10$ the largest error on the interval is about $1.9$, with $n = 20$ about $60$: the polynomials oscillate wildly near $\pm 1$ and get worse as $n$ grows, even though $f$ is perfectly smooth (the trouble comes from its complex poles at $\pm i/5$).

The remedy is to cluster nodes near the ends. The Chebyshev nodes $x_k = \cos\frac{(2k+1)\pi}{2n+2}$, $k = 0, \dots, n$, are the roots of the Chebyshev polynomial $T_{n+1}$, and for them $w = 2^{-n}T_{n+1}$, so $\max_{[-1,1]}|w| = 2^{-n}$, the smallest possible value for a monic polynomial of degree $n+1$. For Runge's function the errors drop to about $0.11$ at $n = 10$ and $0.015$ at $n = 20$, and keep shrinking.

blocks.title: From interpolation to quadrature
blocks.body:
To approximate $\int_a^b f\,dx$ (defined as in [[riemann-integral]]), integrate an interpolating polynomial. With the two nodes $a, b$ the interpolant is a straight line and we get the trapezoidal rule $\frac{b-a}{2}\,(f(a) + f(b))$. With the three nodes $a$, $m = \frac{a+b}{2}$, $b$ we get Simpson's rule $\frac{b-a}{6}\,(f(a) + 4f(m) + f(b))$. Rules built this way from equally spaced nodes are called Newton-Cotes rules.

One wide parabola or line is rarely accurate, so in practice we split $[a,b]$ into $n$ pieces of width $h = (b-a)/n$, with points $x_k = a + kh$, and apply the rule on each. The composite trapezoidal rule is
$$T_h = h\left(\tfrac12 f(x_0) + f(x_1) + \cdots + f(x_{n-1}) + \tfrac12 f(x_n)\right),$$
and for even $n$, applying Simpson's rule on each pair of pieces gives the composite Simpson rule
$$S_h = \frac{h}{3}\big(f(x_0) + 4f(x_1) + 2f(x_2) + 4f(x_3) + \cdots + 4f(x_{n-1}) + f(x_n)\big).$$

The errors are: for $f \in C^2[a,b]$, $\int_a^b f\,dx - T_h = -\frac{(b-a)h^2}{12}f''(\xi)$, and for $f \in C^4[a,b]$, $\int_a^b f\,dx - S_h = -\frac{(b-a)h^4}{180}f^{(4)}(\xi)$, for some $\xi \in [a,b]$. Halving $h$ divides the trapezoidal error by about $4$ and Simpson's error by about $16$. Simpson's rule is exact for cubics, one degree more than its three nodes suggest, because the cubic term's error cancels by symmetry. We prove the trapezoidal formula. The Simpson error formula is stated here without proof: the trapezoidal argument does not carry over directly, because $(x-a)(x-m)(x-b)$ changes sign on $[a,b]$, and the standard proof instead interpolates with $m$ used as a double node.

blocks.title: Error of the trapezoidal rule
blocks.body:
If $f \in C^2[a,b]$ then for some $\xi \in [a,b]$
$$\int_a^b f(x)\,dx - \frac{b-a}{2}\big(f(a) + f(b)\big) = -\frac{(b-a)^3}{12} f''(\xi).$$
Summing over $n$ pieces of width $h$ gives the composite error $-\frac{(b-a)h^2}{12}f''(\xi)$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $p$ be the line through $(a, f(a))$ and $(b, f(b))$, so the trapezoidal value is $\int_a^b p\,dx$. Put $w(x) = (x-a)(x-b)$, which is $\le 0$ on $[a,b]$, and let $m$, $M$ be the minimum and maximum of $f''$ on $[a,b]$. By the interpolation error theorem, for each $x \in (a,b)$ we have $f(x) - p(x) = \tfrac12 f''(\xi_x)\,w(x)$ with $\tfrac12 m \le \tfrac12 f''(\xi_x) \le \tfrac12 M$. Multiplying by $w(x) \le 0$ reverses the inequalities:
$$\tfrac12 M\,w(x) \le f(x) - p(x) \le \tfrac12 m\,w(x).$$
Integrate over $[a,b]$, using $\int_a^b w\,dx = -\frac{(b-a)^3}{6}$:
$$-\tfrac{M}{12}(b-a)^3 \le \int_a^b (f - p)\,dx \le -\tfrac{m}{12}(b-a)^3.$$
So $\int_a^b (f-p)\,dx = -\frac{c}{12}(b-a)^3$ for some $c \in [m, M]$, and by the intermediate value theorem $c = f''(\xi)$ for some $\xi$.

For the composite rule, the errors on the pieces add up to $-\frac{h^3}{12}\sum_{k} f''(\xi_k) = -\frac{h^3 n}{12}\cdot\frac{1}{n}\sum_k f''(\xi_k)$. The average of the $f''(\xi_k)$ lies between $m$ and $M$, so it equals $f''(\xi)$ for some $\xi$, and $h^3 n = (b-a)h^2$.

blocks.title: Gaussian quadrature: choosing the nodes too
blocks.body:
A rule $\sum_{i=1}^{n} w_i f(x_i)$ has $2n$ free numbers, the nodes and the weights, so one may hope to make it exact for all polynomials of degree up to $2n - 1$, a space of dimension $2n$. Gauss showed this is possible. For $n = 2$ on $[-1,1]$, exactness for $1, x, x^2, x^3$ forces $w_1 = w_2 = 1$ and $x_{1,2} = \pm 1/\sqrt3$:
$$\int_{-1}^{1} f(x)\,dx \approx f\!\left(-\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right) + f\!\left(\tfrac{1}{\sqrt3}\right).$$
Two function values, yet every cubic is integrated exactly: for $x^3 - 2x^2 + 5$ the rule gives $\frac{26}{3}$, the true value. It fails first at $x^4$, giving $\frac29$ instead of $\frac25$.

The general construction uses the Legendre polynomials $P_n$: $P_n$ has degree $n$ and is orthogonal on $[-1,1]$ to every polynomial of lower degree, in the sense that $\int_{-1}^1 P_n q\,dx = 0$ when $\deg q < n$ (see [[inner-products]]). One can show $P_n$ has $n$ distinct real roots, all in $(-1,1)$.

blocks.title: Gauss-Legendre quadrature
blocks.body: Let $x_1, \dots, x_n$ be the roots of $P_n$ and let $w_i = \int_{-1}^1 \ell_i(x)\,dx$, where $\ell_i$ are the Lagrange basis polynomials for these nodes. Then $\int_{-1}^1 p(x)\,dx = \sum_{i=1}^n w_i\,p(x_i)$ for every polynomial $p$ of degree at most $2n - 1$. No rule with $n$ nodes is exact for all polynomials of degree $2n$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
By construction the rule integrates the interpolating polynomial of degree at most $n-1$ through the nodes, so it is exact for every polynomial of degree at most $n - 1$. Given $p$ with $\deg p \le 2n - 1$, divide by $P_n$: $p = q P_n + r$ with $\deg q \le n-1$ and $\deg r \le n - 1$. Then $\int_{-1}^1 p = \int_{-1}^1 q P_n + \int_{-1}^1 r = 0 + \sum_i w_i r(x_i)$ by orthogonality and exactness for $r$. On the other side $\sum_i w_i p(x_i) = \sum_i w_i\big(q(x_i)P_n(x_i) + r(x_i)\big) = \sum_i w_i r(x_i)$ since $P_n(x_i) = 0$. The two agree.

For the last claim, given any nodes $x_1, \dots, x_n$, the polynomial $\prod_i (x - x_i)^2$ of degree $2n$ is positive except at the nodes, so its integral is positive, while every rule with these nodes returns $0$ for it.

blocks.title: Example 1: a guaranteed error bound
blocks.body: Interpolate $f(x) = \sin x$ at $0$, $\pi/4$, $\pi/2$ by a quadratic $p_2$. Give an upper bound for $|\sin x - p_2(x)|$ on $[0, \pi/2]$ and compare with the actual error.
blocks.solution:
Here $n = 2$ and $|f'''(\xi)| = |\cos\xi| \le 1$, so $|\sin x - p_2(x)| \le \frac{1}{6}\max|w(x)|$ with $w(x) = x(x-h)(x-2h)$, $h = \pi/4$.

Substitute $x = h + s$, $s \in [-h, h]$: $w = (s+h)s(s-h) = s^3 - h^2 s$. Its derivative $3s^2 - h^2$ vanishes at $s = \pm h/\sqrt3$, where $|w| = \frac{2h^3}{3\sqrt3}$; at $s = \pm h$ it is $0$. So
$$|\sin x - p_2(x)| \le \frac{1}{6}\cdot\frac{2h^3}{3\sqrt3} = \frac{h^3}{9\sqrt3} \approx 0.0311.$$
The actual maximum of $|\sin x - p_2(x)|$ on the interval is about $0.0235$, inside the bound; the bound is not sharp because $|\cos\xi|$ is well below $1$ on much of the interval.

blocks.title: Example 2: computing pi
blocks.body: Since $\int_0^1 \frac{4}{1+x^2}\,dx = 4\arctan 1 = \pi$, approximate $\pi$ with the composite trapezoidal and Simpson rules using $h = \frac14$.
blocks.solution:
The values of $f(x) = 4/(1+x^2)$ at $0, \frac14, \frac12, \frac34, 1$ are
$$4,\quad \tfrac{64}{17},\quad \tfrac{16}{5},\quad \tfrac{64}{25},\quad 2.$$
Trapezoidal rule:
$$T = \tfrac14\left(\tfrac{4 + 2}{2} + \tfrac{64}{17} + \tfrac{16}{5} + \tfrac{64}{25}\right) = \tfrac{5323}{1700} \approx 3.131176,$$
an error of about $-0.0104$. Simpson's rule:
$$S = \tfrac{1}{12}\left(4 + 4\cdot\tfrac{64}{17} + 2\cdot\tfrac{16}{5} + 4\cdot\tfrac{64}{25} + 2\right) = \tfrac{8011}{2550} \approx 3.141569,$$
an error of about $-2.4\times 10^{-5}$. With the same five function values Simpson's rule is more than $400$ times more accurate, as the $h^4$ versus $h^2$ error terms predict.

blocks.title: Example 3: a hidden identity
blocks.body:
Let $x_0, \dots, x_n$ be distinct numbers. Prove that
$$\sum_{i=0}^{n} \frac{x_i^k}{\prod_{j\ne i}(x_i - x_j)} = \begin{cases} 0, & 0 \le k \le n-1,\\ 1, & k = n.\end{cases}$$
blocks.solution:
Interpolate $f(x) = x^k$ with $k \le n$ at the nodes. By uniqueness the interpolant is $x^k$ itself, so
$$x^k = \sum_{i=0}^{n} x_i^k\,\ell_i(x) = \sum_{i=0}^n x_i^k\,\frac{\prod_{j\ne i}(x - x_j)}{\prod_{j \ne i}(x_i - x_j)}.$$
Each $\prod_{j\ne i}(x - x_j)$ is monic of degree $n$, so the coefficient of $x^n$ on the right is exactly the sum in the problem. On the left the coefficient of $x^n$ is $1$ if $k = n$ and $0$ if $k < n$.

For instance with nodes $0, 1, 3$ and $k = 1$: $\frac{0}{(0-1)(0-3)} + \frac{1}{(1-0)(1-3)} + \frac{3}{(3-0)(3-1)} = 0 - \frac12 + \frac12 = 0$. The same sum is the leading coefficient of Newton's form, the divided difference $f[x_0, \dots, x_n]$, which is why divided differences of $x^n$ equal $1$.

blocks.body:
- More nodes is not automatically better. With equally spaced nodes, high-degree interpolation can diverge (Runge's example). Use Chebyshev nodes, or piecewise low-degree pieces such as cubic splines.
- The error formulas need smoothness. For $\int_0^1 \sqrt{x}\,dx$ the derivatives blow up at $0$, and Simpson's rule converges only at the rate $h^{3/2}$, not $h^4$.
- Gauss nodes and weights are tied to the interval $[-1,1]$; for $[a,b]$ substitute $x = \frac{a+b}{2} + \frac{b-a}{2}t$, which multiplies the weights by $\frac{b-a}{2}$.
- For smooth periodic functions integrated over a full period, the plain trapezoidal rule is extremely accurate: for $\int_0^{2\pi} e^{\cos x}\,dx$, eight equally spaced points already give an error near $10^{-6}$. Do not upgrade to Simpson there; it is worse.

Interpolation is the building block of much of numerical analysis. Integrating an interpolant through past slopes gives the Adams methods in [[numerical-odes]]; interpolating a function by a line through two iterates gives the secant method of [[root-finding]]. Fitting a low-degree polynomial to many noisy points, instead of passing through all of them, is [[least-squares]]. The trapezoidal rule's success on periodic functions is explained by [[fourier-series]]: over a full period its error involves only Fourier coefficients of very high order, which are tiny for smooth functions. In high dimensions grids become impossibly large and random sampling takes over ([[monte-carlo]]). Combining $T_h$ and $T_{h/2}$ into $\frac{4T_{h/2} - T_h}{3}$ gives exactly Simpson's rule; repeating this Richardson extrapolation gives Romberg integration.

1. Find, in Newton form, the cubic through $(0,1)$, $(1,2)$, $(2,9)$, $(3,28)$, and identify it.
2. Show directly that Simpson's rule on $[-1,1]$ is exact for $x^3$ but not for $x^4$, and compute its error for $x^4$.
3. How small must $h$ be for the composite trapezoidal rule to approximate $\int_0^1 e^{-x^2}\,dx$ with error below $10^{-6}$? Use $|f''| \le 2$ on $[0,1]$.
4. Derive the weights of the three-point Gauss-Legendre rule, whose nodes are $0$ and $\pm\sqrt{3/5}$.

entry.sum: Most differential equations cannot be solved by formula, so we compute approximate solutions step by step. Euler's method follows the tangent line for a short step $h$: $y_{n+1} = y_n + h f(x_n, y_n)$. A method has order $p$ when its global error shrinks like $h^p$; Euler has order $1$, the classical Runge-Kutta method order $4$, and stiff problems need implicit methods whose stability does not depend on $h$ being tiny.
entry.why: Weather forecasts, spacecraft trajectories, chemical reactors and epidemic models are all differential equations solved numerically; choosing the method and step size decides whether the answer is trustworthy or nonsense.

links.note: Planetary orbits and molecular dynamics are integrated with symplectic methods such as the Stormer-Verlet scheme, which keep energy errors bounded over very long times where ordinary methods drift.
Discretising the space variables of the heat equation turns it into a large stiff system of ODEs (the method of lines), which is then solved with implicit time-stepping.
Computer pictures of chaotic attractors such as the Lorenz system are produced by Runge-Kutta integration, and shadowing theorems explain when such pictures can be trusted.

refs: Süli & Mayers, An Introduction to Numerical Analysis
Iserles, A First Course in the Numerical Analysis of Differential Equations
Hairer, Nørsett & Wanner, Solving Ordinary Differential Equations I

blocks.body:
The equation $y' = x + y$ can be solved by hand, but $y' = x^2 + y^2$ cannot be solved in elementary functions, and neither can the equations for three planets pulling on each other. Yet computers draw their solutions routinely. They do it by marching forward in small steps, using the equation itself to say which way to go next.

We build the simplest such method, prove that it converges, see how better methods gain accuracy for the same work, and meet stiffness, which makes naive methods fail. Equations are first order, $y' = f(x, y)$, $y(a) = y_0$, as in [[ode-first]]; the main tool is [[taylor|Taylor's theorem]].

blocks.title: Euler's method: follow the tangent
blocks.body:
At the starting point $(x_0, y_0)$ the equation tells us the slope of the solution, $f(x_0, y_0)$. Over a short step of length $h$ the solution is close to its tangent line, so we move along the tangent:
$$x_{n+1} = x_n + h, \qquad y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(x_n, y_n).$$
Then we repeat from the new point. The result is a polygon that tries to follow the solution curve through the direction field.

Take $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$, whose solution is $e^x$, with $h = 0.25$. Each step multiplies $y$ by $1 + h = 1.25$, so after four steps $y_4 = 1.25^4 \approx 2.4414$, while $e \approx 2.7183$. The approximation is too low because $e^x$ curves upward and the tangent lines lie below it. With $h = 0.1$ we get $1.1^{10} \approx 2.5937$, and with $h = 0.025$ about $2.6851$: the error, roughly $0.28$, $0.12$, $0.033$, falls in proportion to $h$.

blocks.title: Local and global error
blocks.body:
Two kinds of error must be kept apart. The local error is what one step does wrong when started on the exact solution. By Taylor's theorem
$$y(x_{n+1}) = y(x_n) + h\,y'(x_n) + \tfrac{h^2}{2}y''(\eta_n),$$
and since $y'(x_n) = f(x_n, y(x_n))$, one Euler step from the true value misses by $\tfrac{h^2}{2}y''(\eta_n)$, which is $O(h^2)$.

The global error $e_n = y(x_n) - y_n$ is what we actually care about. Reaching a fixed point $b$ takes $(b-a)/h$ steps, so if local errors simply added up we would expect $\frac{b-a}{h}\cdot O(h^2) = O(h)$. But errors also propagate: a step started from a wrong value follows a neighbouring solution curve, and those may spread apart. The theorem below shows that if $f$ does not change too fast in $y$, the spreading is controlled and the global error really is $O(h)$.

In general, a one-step method $y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,\Phi(x_n, y_n; h)$ has order $p$ if its truncation error $\frac{y(x_{n+1}) - y(x_n)}{h} - \Phi(x_n, y(x_n); h)$ is $O(h^p)$ for smooth solutions. If $\Phi$ is Lipschitz in $y$, the same argument as below then gives a global error $O(h^p)$. Euler's method has order $1$.

blocks.title: Convergence of Euler's method
blocks.body:
Let $f$ be continuous on $[a,b]\times\mathbb{R}$ and Lipschitz in $y$: $|f(x, y) - f(x, z)| \le L|y - z|$ for all $x, y, z$, with $L > 0$. Let $y$ be the solution of $y' = f(x,y)$, $y(a) = y_0$, and suppose $y$ is twice differentiable with $|y''(x)| \le M$ on $[a,b]$. Run Euler's method from $y_0$ with step $h = (b-a)/N$. Then for $n = 0, \dots, N$
$$|y(x_n) - y_n| \le \frac{Mh}{2L}\left(e^{L(x_n - a)} - 1\right).$$
In particular the maximum error is at most $Ch$ with $C = \frac{M}{2L}\left(e^{L(b-a)} - 1\right)$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Write $e_n = y(x_n) - y_n$ and $\tau_n = y(x_{n+1}) - y(x_n) - h f(x_n, y(x_n))$, the local error, so $|\tau_n| \le \frac{Mh^2}{2}$ by the Taylor expansion above. Subtracting the Euler step from the identity $y(x_{n+1}) = y(x_n) + h f(x_n, y(x_n)) + \tau_n$ gives
$$e_{n+1} = e_n + h\big(f(x_n, y(x_n)) - f(x_n, y_n)\big) + \tau_n,$$
and the Lipschitz condition gives
$$|e_{n+1}| \le (1 + hL)|e_n| + \frac{Mh^2}{2}.$$
We claim $|e_n| \le \frac{Mh}{2L}\big((1+hL)^n - 1\big)$. This holds for $n = 0$ since $e_0 = 0$. If it holds for $n$, then
$$|e_{n+1}| \le \frac{Mh}{2L}\big((1+hL)^{n+1} - (1 + hL)\big) + \frac{Mh^2}{2} = \frac{Mh}{2L}\big((1+hL)^{n+1} - 1\big).$$
Finally $1 + hL \le e^{hL}$, so $(1 + hL)^n \le e^{nhL} = e^{L(x_n - a)}$.

blocks.title: Higher-order methods
blocks.body:
Euler uses one slope per step, taken at the start. Using a better average slope across the step raises the order. Heun's method (the improved Euler method) predicts with Euler and then averages the slopes at both ends:
$$k_1 = f(x_n, y_n), \quad k_2 = f(x_n + h, y_n + h k_1), \quad y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{h}{2}(k_1 + k_2).$$
It has order $2$. The classical fourth-order Runge-Kutta method (RK4) samples four slopes:
$$\begin{aligned} k_1 &= f(x_n, y_n), & k_2 &= f\!\left(x_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2 k_1\right),\\ k_3 &= f\!\left(x_n + \tfrac h2,\ y_n + \tfrac h2 k_2\right), & k_4 &= f(x_n + h,\ y_n + h k_3),\end{aligned}$$
$$y_{n+1} = y_n + \tfrac{h}{6}(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4).$$
If $f$ depends on $x$ only, the problem is just $y(b) = y_0 + \int_a^b f$, and these methods become quadrature rules: Euler is a left Riemann sum, Heun is the trapezoidal rule and RK4 is Simpson's rule (see [[interpolation-quadrature]]).

For $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$ on $[0, 1]$ the errors at $x = 1$ are:

- $h = 0.1$: Euler $0.125$, Heun $4.2\times10^{-3}$, RK4 $2.1\times 10^{-6}$;
- $h = 0.05$: Euler $0.065$, Heun $1.1\times10^{-3}$, RK4 $1.4\times 10^{-7}$;
- $h = 0.025$: Euler $0.033$, Heun $2.8\times10^{-4}$, RK4 $8.7\times10^{-9}$.

Halving $h$ divides the errors by about $2$, $4$ and $16$, matching orders $1$, $2$, $4$. RK4 costs four evaluations of $f$ per step, but for the same total work it is vastly more accurate here. Production codes go further and adjust $h$ automatically by comparing two methods of different orders on each step.

blocks.title: Stability and stiffness
blocks.body:
Convergence is a statement about $h \to 0$. With a fixed, practical $h$, a different question matters: does the numerical solution behave qualitatively like the true one? The test case is $y' = -\lambda y$ with $\lambda > 0$, whose solutions decay. Euler gives $y_{n+1} = (1 - h\lambda)y_n$, which decays only if $|1 - h\lambda| < 1$, that is $h < 2/\lambda$. For larger $h$ the numbers oscillate in sign and grow without bound.

An equation is stiff when it contains such a fast-decaying component (large $\lambda$) alongside the slow behaviour we actually want to follow. The fast component dies out almost at once in the true solution, yet it forces explicit methods to use tiny steps for the whole computation. Stiff systems arise from chemical reactions with very different rates and from discretised heat equations.

The cure is an implicit method. Backward Euler uses the slope at the end of the step:
$$y_{n+1} = y_n + h\,f(x_{n+1}, y_{n+1}).$$
Now $y_{n+1}$ appears on both sides, so each step requires solving an equation (usually by Newton's method, see [[root-finding]]). The reward: for $y' = -\lambda y$ it gives $y_{n+1} = y_n/(1 + h\lambda)$, which decays for every $h > 0$.

blocks.title: Systems and long-time behaviour
blocks.body:
Everything above applies to systems $\mathbf{y}' = \mathbf{f}(x, \mathbf{y})$ with vectors in place of numbers, and a second-order equation becomes a system (see [[ode-systems]]). The oscillator $u'' = -u$ becomes $u' = v$, $v' = -u$, whose exact solutions move on circles $u^2 + v^2 = \text{const}$.

Euler's method gives $u_{n+1} = u_n + h v_n$, $v_{n+1} = v_n - h u_n$, and a short computation shows $u_{n+1}^2 + v_{n+1}^2 = (1 + h^2)(u_n^2 + v_n^2)$. The numerical orbit spirals outward: with $100$ steps per period, the energy $u^2 + v^2$ grows by a factor of about $1.48$ every revolution. A tiny change fixes this qualitatively. The symplectic Euler method updates $v$ with the new $u$: $u_{n+1} = u_n + h v_n$, $v_{n+1} = v_n - h u_{n+1}$. It still has order $1$, but it exactly conserves the nearby quantity $u^2 + v^2 + huv$, so for $h < 2$ its orbits stay on a fixed ellipse instead of spiralling outward. For long simulations of mechanical systems, preserving such structure matters more than a high order.

blocks.title: Example 1: Euler's method with an error bound
blocks.body: Apply Euler's method with $h = 0.1$ to $y' = x + y$, $y(0) = 1$, up to $x = 0.3$. Compare with the exact solution $y = 2e^x - x - 1$, and with the bound of the convergence theorem.
blocks.solution:
The steps are $y_{n+1} = y_n + 0.1(x_n + y_n)$:

- $y_1 = 1 + 0.1(0 + 1) = 1.1$;
- $y_2 = 1.1 + 0.1(0.1 + 1.1) = 1.22$;
- $y_3 = 1.22 + 0.1(0.2 + 1.22) = 1.362$.

The exact values are $y(0.1) \approx 1.11034$, $y(0.2) \approx 1.24281$, $y(0.3) \approx 1.39972$, so the errors are about $0.0103$, $0.0228$, $0.0377$, growing as we go.

For the bound: $f(x, y) = x + y$ has Lipschitz constant $L = 1$, and $y'' = 2e^x \le 2e^{0.3} \approx 2.700 = M$ on $[0, 0.3]$. The theorem gives
$$|y(0.3) - y_3| \le \frac{2.700 \cdot 0.1}{2}\left(e^{0.3} - 1\right) \approx 0.0472.$$
The actual error $0.0377$ is below it, as it must be. One Heun step of size $0.1$ gives $y_1 = 1 + 0.05(1 + 1.2) = 1.11$, within $3.5\times10^{-4}$ of $y(0.1)$.

blocks.title: Example 2: why RK4 has order four
blocks.body: Apply one RK4 step to $y' = \lambda y$, $y(0) = 1$, and compare the result with the exact value $e^{\lambda h}$.
blocks.solution:
Put $z = \lambda h$ and $y_n = 1$. Then
$$k_1 = \lambda, \quad k_2 = \lambda\left(1 + \tfrac z2\right), \quad k_3 = \lambda\left(1 + \tfrac z2 + \tfrac{z^2}{4}\right), \quad k_4 = \lambda\left(1 + z + \tfrac{z^2}{2} + \tfrac{z^3}{4}\right).$$
So
$$y_1 = 1 + \tfrac{h}{6}(k_1 + 2k_2 + 2k_3 + k_4) = 1 + z + \frac{z^2}{2} + \frac{z^3}{6} + \frac{z^4}{24}.$$
This is exactly the Taylor polynomial of $e^z$ of degree $4$, so the local error is $\frac{z^5}{120} + \cdots = O(h^5)$, consistent with order $4$. (For general $f$, checking order $4$ means matching all Taylor terms up to $h^4$, which is a much longer calculation.)

The same formula answers the stability question for RK4: with $\lambda < 0$, the method decays only when $|1 + z + z^2/2 + z^3/6 + z^4/24| < 1$, which on the negative real axis means roughly $-2.785 < z < 0$. Higher order does not remove the step-size restriction of explicit methods.

blocks.title: Example 3: a stiff decay
blocks.body: Solve $y' = -20y$, $y(0) = 1$ up to $x = 1.5$ with $h = 0.15$, by explicit and by backward Euler. The exact answer is $e^{-30} \approx 9\times10^{-14}$.
blocks.solution:
Here $h\lambda = 3$. Explicit Euler multiplies by $1 - 3 = -2$ at every step, so after $10$ steps $y_{10} = (-2)^{10} = 1024$. The computed solution oscillates and explodes, while the true solution is essentially zero after the first step. To get decay at all we would need $h < 2/20 = 0.1$, and to get the sign pattern right, $h < 0.05$.

Backward Euler multiplies by $\frac{1}{1 + 3} = \frac14$, so $y_{10} = 4^{-10} \approx 9.5\times10^{-7}$. This is not accurate in relative terms, but it is small and decaying, which is the correct qualitative behaviour. In a stiff system this is what we need: the fast component is damped harmlessly while $h$ is chosen to follow the slow ones.

blocks.title: Example 4: Euler's method and the number e
blocks.body: Euler's method for $y' = y$, $y(0) = 1$ with $h = 1/n$ gives $y_n = (1 + 1/n)^n$ at $x = 1$. Prove that this is always less than $e$, and that the error satisfies $n\big(e - (1 + 1/n)^n\big) \to e/2$.
blocks.solution:
For $t \ne 0$ we have $1 + t < e^t$ (the exponential lies above its tangent line at $0$, by convexity). With $t = 1/n$ this gives $(1 + 1/n)^n < (e^{1/n})^n = e$.

For the rate, use $\ln(1 + t) = t - \frac{t^2}{2} + O(t^3)$:
$$\ln\left(1 + \tfrac1n\right)^n = n\left(\tfrac1n - \tfrac{1}{2n^2} + O(n^{-3})\right) = 1 - \frac{1}{2n} + O(n^{-2}).$$
Exponentiating, $(1 + 1/n)^n = e\cdot e^{-1/(2n) + O(n^{-2})} = e\left(1 - \frac{1}{2n} + O(n^{-2})\right)$. Hence $e - (1+1/n)^n = \frac{e}{2n} + O(n^{-2})$, and multiplying by $n$ gives the limit $e/2$.

So the global error is about $\frac{e}{2}h$ with $h = 1/n$ (compare the error $0.125$ at $n = 10$ with $e/20 \approx 0.136$), while the general theorem gives the larger constant $\frac{M}{2L}(e^{L} - 1) = \frac{e}{2}(e - 1) \approx 2.34$ (with $L = 1$, $M = e$).

blocks.body:
- A smooth-looking numerical solution is not necessarily accurate. Always repeat the computation with $h/2$ and compare; the difference estimates the error.
- Order describes how the error shrinks as $h \to 0$; it says nothing about whether a given $h$ is small enough. Stiff problems can make every explicit method useless at reasonable step sizes.
- Rounding error grows as $h$ shrinks, because the number of steps grows. Making $h$ extremely small in an order-$1$ method can make results worse, not better.
- Near a solution that blows up in finite time, such as $y' = y^2$, $y(0) = 1$ at $x = 1$, a numerical method marches straight past the singularity and reports finite numbers. The theorem's hypotheses (global Lipschitz constant, bounded $y''$) fail there.

Linear multistep methods (Adams-Bashforth, Adams-Moulton, BDF) reuse past slopes instead of new evaluations; they are derived by integrating interpolating polynomials, as in [[interpolation-quadrature]]. The existence proof for solutions by Picard iteration, an instance of the [[contraction-mapping]] principle, uses the same Lipschitz condition as our convergence theorem. Discretising space in the [[heat-equation]] or [[wave-equation]] produces large systems of ODEs, the first stiff and the second oscillatory, which is where the stability theory of this page is used most. Numerical solutions are also the main experimental tool for [[phase-plane]] portraits, [[limit-cycles]] and [[chaos]].

entry.sum: A linear program asks for the largest or smallest value of a linear expression such as $2x + 3y$ when the variables must satisfy linear inequalities. The allowed points form a convex polygon or polyhedron, and if an optimum exists it is attained at a corner, which is what the simplex method exploits. Every linear program has a dual, and the duality theorem says that if one of the two has an optimum then so does the other, with the same value, so any optimum comes with a short certificate proving it.
key: \max\{\,c^{\mathsf T}x : Ax \le b,\ x \ge 0\,\} = \min\{\,b^{\mathsf T}y : A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c,\ y \ge 0\,\}
Ax \le b,\ x \ge 0,\ A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c,\ y \ge 0 \implies c^{\mathsf T}x \le b^{\mathsf T}y
\text{on a nonempty bounded feasible region the optimum is attained at a vertex}
entry.why: Airlines schedule crews, refineries blend fuels and supply chains route goods by solving linear programs with millions of variables, and duality turns optimal solutions into prices that say what each scarce resource is worth.

links.note: Konig's theorem that maximum matchings and minimum vertex covers in bipartite graphs have equal size is linear programming duality applied to a problem whose optimal solutions are automatically integers.

Feasible regions are convex polyhedra and the simplex method walks along their edges, which makes questions about the diameters of polytopes, such as the Hirsch conjecture disproved by Santos in 2010, questions about this algorithm.

refs: Matoušek & Gärtner, Understanding and Using Linear Programming

blocks.body:
A small bakery makes trays of bread and trays of cake. Each tray of either kind spends one hour in the oven, and the oven is free for $4$ hours. A tray of bread needs $1$ hour of a baker's time and a tray of cake needs $3$, and the baker has $6$ hours. A tray of bread earns a profit of $2$ and a tray of cake a profit of $3$. How many of each should be made?

Problems with a linear goal and linear limits are called linear programs (program means plan, not computer code). We solve small ones by drawing, see why the answer is at a corner and how the simplex method finds it in large problems, and use duality to prove that an answer is optimal. You need [[solving-inequalities]] and a little of [[linear-systems]].

blocks.title: Writing down the problem
blocks.body:
Let $x$ be the number of trays of bread and $y$ the number of trays of cake (we allow fractions; think of them as average daily amounts). The problem is:
$$\text{maximise } 2x + 3y \quad\text{subject to}\quad x + y \le 4,\quad x + 3y \le 6,\quad x \ge 0,\quad y \ge 0.$$

The ingredients are decision variables ($x$, $y$), a linear objective to maximise or minimise, and linear constraints. A point satisfying all constraints is called feasible, and the set of all feasible points is the feasible region. It may be empty (the constraints contradict each other), and the objective may be unbounded on it (it can be made as large as we like). Otherwise there is an optimal solution.

blocks.title: Solving by drawing
blocks.body:
With two variables we can draw. Each inequality is a half-plane: $x + y \le 4$ is everything on or below the line $x + y = 4$, and $x + 3y \le 6$ is everything on or below the line through $(6, 0)$ and $(0, 2)$. Together with $x, y \ge 0$, the feasible region is the quadrilateral with corners
$$(0,0),\quad (4, 0),\quad (3, 1),\quad (0, 2).$$
The corner $(3,1)$ is where the two lines cross: subtracting $x + y = 4$ from $x + 3y = 6$ gives $2y = 2$.

Now picture the objective. The points where $2x + 3y = k$ form a line, and changing $k$ slides it parallel to itself. Start with a small $k$ and slide the line upward as far as it can go while still touching the region. The last point it touches is a corner. Checking the corners:
$$2\cdot 0 + 3\cdot 0 = 0,\quad 2\cdot 4 + 0 = 8,\quad 2\cdot 3 + 3\cdot 1 = 9,\quad 0 + 3\cdot 2 = 6.$$
The best plan is $3$ trays of bread and $1$ of cake, with profit $9$.

blocks.title: The corner principle
blocks.body: If the feasible region of a linear program in two variables is a nonempty bounded polygon, then the objective attains its maximum (and its minimum) at a corner of the polygon. The same holds in any number of variables, with corners of a bounded polyhedron, called vertices.

blocks.title: Proof in two variables
blocks.body:
First look at a single segment from $P$ to $Q$. Its points are $P + t(Q - P)$ for $0 \le t \le 1$, and a linear objective $f$ takes the values $f(P) + t\,(f(Q) - f(P))$ there, which change steadily with $t$. So on a segment, $f$ is largest at one of the two endpoints.

The feasible region is an intersection of half-planes, so it is convex: the segment between two of its points stays inside it. Take any feasible point $R$. Draw any line through $R$; because the region is bounded, the part of the line inside the region is a segment whose two endpoints lie on the boundary. By the first paragraph, $f(R)$ is at most $f$ at one of these endpoints, call it $S$. Now $S$ lies on an edge of the polygon, which is itself a segment between two corners, so $f(S)$ is at most $f$ at one of these corners. Hence $f(R) \le f(\text{some corner})$ for every feasible $R$, and the largest of the finitely many corner values is the maximum. The minimum is handled the same way.

blocks.title: The simplex method
blocks.body:
With $50$ variables and $100$ constraints a polyhedron can have astronomically many vertices, so checking them all is hopeless. Dantzig's simplex method (1947) walks from vertex to vertex along edges, each time improving the objective, and stops when no edge leads uphill.

Here is the walk for the bakery. Start at $(0,0)$, profit $0$. Cake earns more per tray, so increase $y$ while keeping $x = 0$. The oven allows $y \le 4$, but the baker allows only $y \le 2$, so we stop at the vertex $(0,2)$, profit $6$. Now move along the baker's line $x + 3y = 6$, increasing $x$. On this line $y = (6 - x)/3$, so the profit is $2x + (6 - x) = x + 6$, which increases with $x$. We continue until the oven constraint $x + y \le 4$ blocks us, at $(3, 1)$, profit $9$. From $(3,1)$ both edges lead downhill: along the oven line the profit is $2x + 3(4 - x) = 12 - x$, falling toward $(4,0)$, and going back along the baker's line lowers $x + 6$. So $(3,1)$ is optimal.

On a computer the walk is done with row operations as in Gaussian elimination, after adding a slack variable to each constraint (for example $x + y + s_1 = 4$, $s_1 \ge 0$, where $s_1$ is unused oven time). The simplex method is very fast in practice, although Klee and Minty (1972) built deformed cubes in $n$ dimensions on which Dantzig's original pivoting rule visits all $2^n$ vertices; the ellipsoid method (Khachiyan, 1979) and interior-point methods (Karmarkar, 1984) are provably fast in the worst case.

blocks.title: Duality: proving that an answer is optimal
blocks.body:
How could the bakery convince a sceptic that $9$ is truly the best, without the picture? Add the constraints with suitable multipliers. Take $\frac32$ of the oven constraint and $\frac12$ of the baker constraint:
$$\tfrac32(x + y) + \tfrac12(x + 3y) = 2x + 3y \le \tfrac32\cdot 4 + \tfrac12\cdot 6 = 9.$$
So no feasible plan beats $9$, and $(3,1)$ achieves it. The multipliers are a certificate of optimality.

Which multipliers work? For any $u, v \ge 0$ we have $u(x + y) + v(x + 3y) \le 4u + 6v$. The left side is $(u + v)x + (u + 3v)y$, and it is at least $2x + 3y$ whenever $u + v \ge 2$ and $u + 3v \ge 3$ (because $x, y \ge 0$). The best bound comes from a new linear program, the dual:
$$\text{minimise } 4u + 6v \quad\text{subject to}\quad u + v \ge 2,\quad u + 3v \ge 3,\quad u, v \ge 0.$$
Its optimum is $u = \frac32$, $v = \frac12$ with value $9$: the same number as the original problem.

The dual has a meaning. Someone wants to rent the oven and the baker, paying $u$ per oven hour and $v$ per baker hour. The bakery agrees only if the hours used for one tray earn at least as much rented out as baked, which is exactly the dual's constraints; the renter wants to pay as little as possible. The optimal values $u = \frac32$, $v = \frac12$ are called shadow prices: one extra oven hour would raise the best profit by $\frac32$ (from $9$ to $10.5$), and one extra baker hour by $\frac12$, as long as the same two constraints stay the binding ones.

blocks.title: Weak and strong duality
blocks.body:
Let $A$ be an $m \times n$ matrix, $b \in \mathbb{R}^m$, $c \in \mathbb{R}^n$. The primal problem is to maximise $c^{\mathsf T}x$ subject to $Ax \le b$, $x \ge 0$, and the dual problem is to minimise $b^{\mathsf T}y$ subject to $A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c$, $y \ge 0$ (inequalities between vectors hold entry by entry).

1. Weak duality: if $x$ is primal feasible and $y$ is dual feasible, then $c^{\mathsf T}x \le b^{\mathsf T}y$.
2. Strong duality (stated here without proof): if the primal has an optimal solution, so does the dual, and the two optimal values are equal.

blocks.title: Proof of weak duality
blocks.body:
Since $x \ge 0$ and $A^{\mathsf T}y \ge c$ entry by entry, $c^{\mathsf T}x \le (A^{\mathsf T}y)^{\mathsf T}x = y^{\mathsf T}(Ax)$. Since $y \ge 0$ and $Ax \le b$, $y^{\mathsf T}(Ax) \le y^{\mathsf T}b$. Together, $c^{\mathsf T}x \le b^{\mathsf T}y$.

Strong duality is deeper; its standard proofs go through the simplex method or through a separation theorem for convex sets (Farkas' lemma), and we do not give one here. A useful consequence of the two parts together is complementary slackness: at optimal $x$ and $y$, every constraint that is not tight has dual price $0$, and every positive dual price belongs to a tight constraint. For instance, if the bakery's oven had $10$ free hours, the best plan would be $6$ trays of bread (profit $12$) with $4$ oven hours unused, and the oven's shadow price drops to $0$.

blocks.title: Example 1: a cheapest diet
blocks.body: Food A costs $3$ per portion and gives $1$ unit of protein and $3$ units of vitamins. Food B costs $4$ per portion and gives $2$ units of protein and $1$ unit of vitamins. We need at least $4$ units of protein and $6$ of vitamins. Find the cheapest combination.
blocks.solution:
With $x$ portions of A and $y$ of B: minimise $3x + 4y$ subject to $x + 2y \ge 4$, $3x + y \ge 6$, $x, y \ge 0$.

The feasible region lies above both lines and is unbounded, but costs are positive, so a minimum exists. Its corners are $(0, 6)$ on the $y$-axis, $(4, 0)$ on the $x$-axis, and the crossing of the two lines: from $3x + y = 6$ we get $y = 6 - 3x$, and then $x + 12 - 6x = 4$ gives $x = \frac85$, $y = \frac65$.

Costs: $(0,6)$ gives $24$, $(4,0)$ gives $12$, and $\left(\frac85, \frac65\right)$ gives $\frac{24}{5} + \frac{24}{5} = \frac{48}{5} = 9.6$. The cheapest diet is $1.6$ portions of A and $1.2$ of B.

The corner principle was stated for bounded regions, so we should check that nothing further out is cheaper. Here a certificate does it: adding $\frac95$ times the protein constraint and $\frac25$ times the vitamin constraint gives $3x + 4y \ge \frac{36}{5} + \frac{12}{5} = \frac{48}{5}$ for every feasible point.

blocks.title: Example 2: shipping at least cost
blocks.body: Bakery A has $30$ crates and bakery B has $20$. Shop P needs $25$ crates and shop Q needs $25$. The cost per crate is $4$ from A to P, $6$ from A to Q, $5$ from B to P and $3$ from B to Q. How should the crates be shipped?
blocks.solution:
Let $a$ be the number of crates from A to P. Then everything else is forced: A sends $30 - a$ to Q, P needs $25 - a$ more from B, and Q needs $25 - (30 - a) = a - 5$ from B. All four amounts must be at least $0$, which gives $5 \le a \le 25$.

The total cost is
$$4a + 6(30 - a) + 5(25 - a) + 3(a - 5) = 290 - 4a,$$
which is smallest when $a$ is largest. So $a = 25$: A sends $25$ to P and $5$ to Q, B sends $20$ to Q and none to P, for a cost of $100 + 30 + 60 = 190$.

This is a transportation problem. The supply and demand equations left one free variable, so the feasible region was a segment and the optimum sat at an end. When supplies and demands are whole numbers, the vertices of a transportation problem always have whole-number coordinates, so solving it as a linear program never splits a crate.

blocks.title: Example 3: a bound by adding inequalities
blocks.body: Nonnegative numbers $x, y, z$ satisfy $x + y \le 3$, $y + z \le 4$ and $z + x \le 5$. Find the largest possible value of $x + y + z$, and of $x + y + 2z$.
blocks.solution:
Adding all three constraints gives $2(x + y + z) \le 12$, so $x + y + z \le 6$. Equality needs all three constraints tight: $x + y = 3$, $y + z = 4$, $z + x = 5$, which gives $x = 2$, $y = 1$, $z = 3$, all nonnegative. So the maximum is $6$, and the dual multipliers are $\left(\frac12, \frac12, \frac12\right)$.

For $x + y + 2z$, add the second and third constraints: $x + y + 2z \le 9$. Equality needs $y + z = 4$ and $z + x = 5$, so $x = 5 - z$ and $y = 4 - z$; the first constraint becomes $9 - 2z \le 3$, so $z \ge 3$, and $y \ge 0$ needs $z \le 4$. Every $z$ in $[3, 4]$ works, for example $(2, 1, 3)$ and $(1, 0, 4)$, both giving $9$. The maximum is $9$, attained along a whole edge of the feasible polyhedron between two vertices. This is allowed by the corner principle: the maximum is attained at a vertex, but perhaps not only there.

blocks.body:
- Checking only the corners is valid only when an optimum exists. If the region is unbounded the objective may have no maximum at all; if the region is empty there is nothing to optimise.
- Rounding a fractional optimum to whole numbers can give an infeasible or far from optimal plan. Problems that require integer answers (integer programming) are much harder in general: the decision version is NP-complete.
- Not every crossing of two constraint lines is a corner: $x + 3y = 6$ meets $y = 0$ at $(6, 0)$, which violates $x + y \le 4$. Always check feasibility.
- A shadow price is valid only for small changes. Increase the oven time enough and a different pair of constraints becomes binding, and the price changes.

Linear programming is the simplest case of [[convex-optimisation]], where duality carries over and interior-point methods are the main algorithms; its multipliers are the inequality version of [[lagrange-multipliers]]. Maximum flow and minimum cut in [[network-flows]] are a dual pair of linear programs, and so are maximum matching and minimum vertex cover in bipartite graphs (see [[cycles-matchings]]). The feasible regions are convex sets, the subject of [[convexity]]. Von Neumann's minimax theorem for two-player zero-sum games is equivalent to linear programming duality. On the computational side, see [[algorithms]] and the discussion of integer programming in [[p-vs-np]].

1. Maximise $x + 2y$ subject to $x + y \le 5$, $y \le 3$, $2x + y \le 8$, $x, y \ge 0$, and find multipliers that prove your answer optimal.
2. Write down the dual of: maximise $5x + 4y$ subject to $2x + y \le 8$, $x + 2y \le 7$, $x, y \ge 0$. Solve both problems and check that the optimal values agree.
3. Show that the constraints $x + y \ge 5$, $x \le 2$, $y \le 2$ have no solution, by adding suitable multiples of them to reach a contradiction.
4. For the bakery, find the profit per tray of cake at which the best plan changes from $(3, 1)$ to $(0, 2)$.

entry.sum: A convex optimisation problem minimises a convex function over a convex set, described by convex inequality constraints $f_i(x) \le 0$ and linear equations $Ax = b$. Convexity makes every local minimum global, turns the first-order condition into a complete test for optimality, and gives a dual problem whose value equals the primal one under Slater's condition, which leads to the KKT conditions and to algorithms that provably find the optimum.
key: \text{minimise } f_0(x) \ \text{ subject to } \ f_i(x) \le 0\ (i = 1, \dots, m),\ \ Ax = b, \qquad f_0, \dots, f_m \text{ convex}
f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y - x) \quad \text{for all } x, y

g(\lambda, 
u) = \inf_x L(x, \lambda, 
u) \le p^\star \ \ (\lambda \ge 0), \qquad \max_{\lambda \ge 0,\,
u} g(\lambda, 
u) = p^\star 	ext{ under Slater's condition}
entry.why: Whether a problem is convex is the practical line between optimisation problems that can be solved reliably at scale and those that in general cannot; least squares, linear programs, support vector machines, portfolio selection and many control and signal-processing tasks are all convex.

links.note: The lasso, logistic regression and maximum likelihood for exponential families are convex problems, so their estimates are global optima that standard solvers compute reliably.
Support vector machines are trained by solving a convex quadratic program, and the KKT conditions explain why only the support vectors, the points on or inside the margin, determine the classifier.

blocks.body:
Most optimisation problems are hard because a search can get stuck: a point may be better than everything nearby yet far from the best overall, and there is no local way to tell. Convex problems are exactly the ones where this cannot happen. If the function is bowl-shaped and the allowed region has no dents, any point that cannot be improved locally is a global optimum, and a simple first-order test certifies it.

We state the standard form, prove that local optima are global, give the first-order test, and develop Lagrangian duality and the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker (KKT) conditions, which extend [[lagrange-multipliers]] to inequality constraints. Background: [[convexity]] and [[inner-products]].

blocks.title: Convex sets and functions, briefly
blocks.body:
A set $C \subseteq \mathbb{R}^n$ is convex if the segment between any two of its points lies in it. A function $f$ is convex if $f(\theta x + (1-\theta)y) \le \theta f(x) + (1 - \theta)f(y)$ for all $x, y$ and $\theta \in [0,1]$: the graph lies below its chords.

The examples that matter most in practice are: affine functions $a^{\mathsf T}x + b$; norms $\|x\|$; quadratics $x^{\mathsf T}Qx$ with $Q$ positive semidefinite; $-\log x$ and $e^{x}$ in one variable; and $\log(e^{x_1} + \cdots + e^{x_n})$. New convex functions come from old ones by taking nonnegative combinations, maxima, and composition with affine maps, so $\max_i (a_i^{\mathsf T}x + b_i)$ and $\|Ax - b\|$ are convex.

If $f$ is convex, every sublevel set $\{x : f(x) \le t\}$ is convex. Hence a region described by convex inequalities $f_i(x) \le 0$ together with linear equations is convex: it is an intersection of convex sets.

blocks.title: Convex optimisation problem
blocks.body:
A problem of the form
$$\text{minimise } f_0(x) \quad\text{subject to}\quad f_i(x) \le 0\ \ (i = 1, \dots, m), \qquad Ax = b,$$
where $x \in \mathbb{R}^n$ and $f_0, f_1, \dots, f_m$ are convex functions. Its optimal value is $p^\star = \inf\{f_0(x) : x \text{ feasible}\}$. Equivalently: minimise a convex function over a convex set given by convex inequalities and affine equations. (Maximising a concave function is the same thing, after a change of sign.)

blocks.title: Local minima are global
blocks.body: Let $f$ be convex and $C$ convex. If $x^\star \in C$ is a local minimiser of $f$ on $C$, it is a global minimiser. The set of global minimisers is convex, and if $f$ is strictly convex there is at most one.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Suppose some $y \in C$ had $f(y) < f(x^\star)$. For $\theta \in (0, 1]$ the point $z_\theta = (1 - \theta)x^\star + \theta y$ lies in $C$, and
$$f(z_\theta) \le (1 - \theta)f(x^\star) + \theta f(y) < f(x^\star).$$
As $\theta \to 0$, $z_\theta$ comes arbitrarily close to $x^\star$, so $x^\star$ would not be a local minimiser.

If $x$ and $y$ are both global minimisers with value $p^\star$, then $f(z_\theta) \le p^\star$ for every $\theta \in [0,1]$, so the whole segment consists of minimisers. If $f$ is strictly convex and $x \ne y$, then $f(z_{1/2}) < p^\star$, which is impossible.

blocks.title: First-order conditions
blocks.body:
Let $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$ be differentiable.

1. $f$ is convex if and only if $f(y) \ge f(x) + \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y - x)$ for all $x, y$: the graph lies above every tangent plane.
2. If $f$ is convex and $C$ is convex, then $x^\star \in C$ minimises $f$ over $C$ if and only if $\nabla f(x^\star)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) \ge 0$ for every $y \in C$. When $C = \mathbb{R}^n$ this says $\nabla f(x^\star) = 0$.

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
1. If $f$ is convex, then for $t \in (0, 1]$
$$ rac{f(x + t(y - x)) - f(x)}{t} \le  rac{(1-t)f(x) + t f(y) - f(x)}{t} = f(y) - f(x).$$
As $t 	o 0^+$ the left side tends to the directional derivative $
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y - x)$, giving the inequality. Conversely, assume the inequality, let $z = 	heta x + (1-	heta)y$, and apply it at $z$: $f(x) \ge f(z) + 
abla f(z)^{\mathsf T}(x - z)$ and $f(y) \ge f(z) + 
abla f(z)^{\mathsf T}(y - z)$. Multiply by $	heta$ and $1 - 	heta$ and add; since $	heta(x - z) + (1 - 	heta)(y - z) = 0$, we get $	heta f(x) + (1-	heta)f(y) \ge f(z)$.

2. If the condition holds, part 1 gives $f(y) \ge f(x^\star) + 
abla f(x^\star)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) \ge f(x^\star)$ for all $y \in C$. If it fails for some $y \in C$, then $\varphi(t) = f(x^\star + t(y - x^\star))$ has $\varphi'(0) = 
abla f(x^\star)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) < 0$, so $\varphi(t) < \varphi(0)$ for small $t > 0$; those points lie in $C$ by convexity, so $x^\star$ is not a minimiser.

blocks.title: Lagrangian duality
blocks.body:
Attach a multiplier $\lambda_i \ge 0$ to each inequality and a multiplier $
u_j$ to each equation, and form the Lagrangian
$$L(x, \lambda, 
u) = f_0(x) + \sum_{i=1}^m \lambda_i f_i(x) + 
u^{\mathsf T}(Ax - b).$$
The dual function is $g(\lambda, 
u) = \inf_x L(x, \lambda, 
u)$, the infimum over all $x$ with no constraints (it may be $-\infty$).

Weak duality is one line. If $x$ is feasible and $\lambda \ge 0$, every added term is $\le 0$ (since $f_i(x) \le 0$ and $Ax = b$), so $g(\lambda, 
u) \le L(x, \lambda, 
u) \le f_0(x)$. Taking the infimum over feasible $x$: $g(\lambda, 
u) \le p^\star$. Every choice of multipliers gives a lower bound, and the dual problem asks for the best one: maximise $g(\lambda, 
u)$ subject to $\lambda \ge 0$, with optimal value $d^\star \le p^\star$. Since $g$ is an infimum of functions that are affine in $(\lambda, 
u)$, it is concave, so the dual is itself a convex problem, whether or not the primal is.

For convex problems the gap $p^\star - d^\star$ is usually zero. The standard sufficient condition is Slater's condition: there is a strictly feasible point, some $x$ with $f_i(x) < 0$ for all $i$ and $Ax = b$. If a convex problem satisfies Slater's condition, then $d^\star = p^\star$ and, when $p^\star$ is finite, the dual optimum is attained. We state this theorem without proof; the standard proof separates two convex sets in $\mathbb{R}^{m+1}$ by a hyperplane. For linear programs ([[linear-programming]]) no Slater condition is needed: strong duality holds whenever the primal has an optimum.

blocks.title: Karush-Kuhn-Tucker conditions
Proof of (a)
blocks.body:
For fixed $\lambda^\star \ge 0$ and $
u^\star$, the function $x \mapsto L(x, \lambda^\star, 
u^\star)$ is convex (a nonnegative combination of convex functions plus an affine one), and condition 4 says its gradient vanishes at $x^\star$. By the first-order conditions, $x^\star$ minimises it, so
$$g(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star) = L(x^\star, \lambda^\star, 
u^\star) = f_0(x^\star) + \sum_i \lambda^\star_i f_i(x^\star) + 
u^{\star\mathsf T}(Ax^\star - b) = f_0(x^\star),$$
using conditions 3 and 1. So a feasible point and a dual feasible point have the same value. By weak duality $f_0(x^\star) = g(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star) \le d^\star \le p^\star \le f_0(x^\star)$, so all are equal: $x^\star$ is primal optimal and $(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star)$ is dual optimal.

Part (b) rests on Slater's theorem, quoted above without proof: since $p^\star = f_0(x^\star)$ is finite, it supplies a dual optimum $(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star)$ with $g(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star) = f_0(x^\star)$. Then the chain $f_0(x^\star) = g(\lambda^\star, 
u^\star) \le L(x^\star, \lambda^\star, 
u^\star) \le f_0(x^\star)$ forces both inequalities to be equalities. The second equality gives $\sum_i \lambda^\star_i f_i(x^\star) = 0$, a sum of nonpositive terms, hence condition 3; the first says $x^\star$ minimises $L(\cdot, \lambda^\star, 
u^\star)$, hence condition 4.

blocks.title: The main problem classes and how they are solved
Example 1: the closest point of a half-plane
blocks.body: Minimise $x^2 + y^2$ subject to $x + y \ge 2$. Solve with the KKT conditions, then compute the dual function and check that there is no duality gap.
blocks.solution:
Write the constraint as $f_1(x,y) = 2 - x - y \le 0$; Slater holds (take $(2,2)$). The Lagrangian is $L = x^2 + y^2 + \lambda(2 - x - y)$. Stationarity gives $2x = \lambda$, $2y = \lambda$. If $\lambda = 0$ then $x = y = 0$, which is infeasible. So $\lambda > 0$, complementary slackness forces $x + y = 2$, hence $x = y = 1$ and $\lambda = 2 \ge 0$. All four KKT conditions hold, so $(1,1)$ is optimal with $p^\star = 2$. Geometrically, $(1,1)$ is the point of the line $x + y = 2$ nearest the origin.

For the dual, minimise $L$ over all $(x, y)$: the minimum is at $x = y = \lambda/2$, so
$$g(\lambda) = \frac{\lambda^2}{4} + \frac{\lambda^2}{4} + \lambda(2 - \lambda) = 2\lambda - \frac{\lambda^2}{2}.$$
This concave function is largest at $\lambda = 2$, with $g(2) = 2 = p^\star$. Every other $\lambda \ge 0$ gives a smaller lower bound, for instance $g(1) = 1.5$.

blocks.title: Example 2: a weighted sum of squares, with and without a floor
blocks.body: Minimise $x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2$ subject to $x + y + z = 1$. Then solve the same problem with the extra constraint $z \ge \frac14$.
blocks.solution:
Without the floor, stationarity of $L = x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 + 
u(x + y + z - 1)$ gives $2x = 4y = 6z = -
u$. So $x : y : z = 6 : 3 : 2$, and $x + y + z = 1$ gives $(x,y,z) = \left( rac{6}{11},  rac{3}{11},  rac{2}{11}ight)$, with value
$$ rac{36 + 18 + 12}{121} =  rac{6}{11}.$$
The objective is strictly convex, so this is the unique global minimum; Cauchy-Schwarz confirms it: $1 = (x + y + z)^2 \le (x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2)\left(1 +  rac12 +  rac13ight)$, so the value is at least $ rac{6}{11}$.

With the floor, the old optimum has $z =  rac{2}{11} <  rac14$, so it is infeasible, and we guess that the new constraint $f_1 =  rac14 - z \le 0$ is active: $z =  rac14$. Then minimise $x^2 + 2y^2$ with $x + y =  rac34$: stationarity gives $x = 2y$, so $y =  rac14$, $x =  rac12$, and the value is $ rac14 +  rac18 +  rac{3}{16} =  rac{9}{16}$.

To confirm, find the multipliers. Stationarity of $x^2 + 2y^2 + 3z^2 + \lambda( rac14 - z) + 
u(x + y + z - 1)$ reads $2x + 
u = 0$, $4y + 
u = 0$, $6z - \lambda + 
u = 0$. With $x =  rac12$, $y =  rac14$, $z =  rac14$ the first two give $
u = -1$, and the third gives $\lambda =  rac32 - 1 =  rac12 \ge 0$. Complementary slackness holds because the constraint is tight. By part (a) of the KKT theorem, $\left( rac12,  rac14,  rac14ight)$ is optimal. The multiplier $\lambda =  rac12$ is the rate at which the optimal value rises as the floor is raised.

blocks.title: Example 3: projection onto a convex set
blocks.body: Let $C$ be closed and convex and $a$ a point. Show that $x^\star \in C$ is the point of $C$ closest to $a$ if and only if $(a - x^\star)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) \le 0$ for every $y \in C$. Use this to find the closest point to $a$ in the set $\{x \in \mathbb{R}^n : x \ge 0\}$.
blocks.solution:
Minimise $f(x) = \frac12\|x - a\|^2$ over $C$; here $\nabla f(x) = x - a$. By the first-order conditions, $x^\star$ is optimal if and only if $(x^\star - a)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) \ge 0$ for all $y \in C$, which is the stated condition after a change of sign. Geometrically: the angle at $x^\star$ between the directions to $a$ and to any other point of $C$ is at least $90^\circ$. (A closest point exists because $C$ is closed, and it is unique because $f$ is strictly convex.)

For $C = \{x \ge 0\}$, guess $x^\star_i = \max(a_i, 0)$. Then $(a - x^\star)_i$ is $0$ when $a_i \ge 0$, and equals $a_i < 0$ when $a_i < 0$, in which case $x^\star_i = 0$. So
$$(a - x^\star)^{\mathsf T}(y - x^\star) = \sum_{i:\,a_i < 0} a_i\,y_i \le 0 \quad\text{for all } y \ge 0.$$
The guess is right: projecting onto the nonnegative orthant just sets the negative coordinates to zero. For $a = (3, -1, 2, -5)$ the projection is $(3, 0, 2, 0)$.

blocks.body:
- Strong duality and the KKT theorem part (b) need a constraint qualification such as Slater's condition. For minimise $x$ subject to $x^2 \le 0$, the only feasible point is $x = 0$, so $p^\star = 0$; the dual function is $g(\lambda) = \inf_x (x + \lambda x^2) = -\frac{1}{4\lambda}$ for $\lambda > 0$, whose supremum $0$ is never attained, and no $\lambda$ satisfies stationarity $1 + 2\lambda\cdot 0 = 0$. Slater fails because no $x$ has $x^2 < 0$.
- The constraint functions must be convex and the equations affine. The set $\{x : x^2 = 1\}$ is not convex even though $x^2$ is.
- A minimiser may fail to exist even for convex problems: $e^x$ on $\mathbb{R}$ has infimum $0$ but no minimiser.

[[linear-programming]] is the polyhedral special case, and its duality theorem is the model for everything here. Unconstrained convex problems are the setting in which the convergence guarantees of [[gradient-descent]] are proved, with strong convexity controlling the rate. [[least-squares]] is the simplest quadratic program, and the projection characterisation in Example 3 is the convex-set version of orthogonal projection in [[hilbert-spaces]]. The separating hyperplane theorem behind Slater's condition is a finite-dimensional cousin of the [[hahn-banach]] theorem. The Legendre-Fenchel conjugate behind convex duality is also the transform from Lagrangian to Hamiltonian mechanics in [[calculus-of-variations]].

entry.sum: Gradient descent minimises a function by repeatedly stepping against its gradient, $x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\,\nabla f(x_k)$, the direction of steepest local decrease. With step $\eta = 1/L$ for an $L$-smooth function each step lowers $f$ by at least $\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2/(2L)$; for $\mu$-strongly convex functions the gap to the minimum shrinks geometrically at rate $1 - \mu/L$. Stochastic gradient descent replaces the gradient by a cheap random estimate, which is how large machine-learning models are trained.
entry.why: It needs only gradients, which can be computed for functions of billions of variables, so it is the workhorse for fitting statistical models and training neural networks; its convergence theory explains why badly scaled problems are slow and how step sizes should be chosen.

links.note: Logistic regression and other maximum-likelihood fits are computed by gradient methods, and stochastic gradient descent is a special case of the Robbins-Monro stochastic approximation scheme.

Gradient descent on $\frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Ax - b^{\mathsf T}x$ with $A$ symmetric positive definite is an iterative solver for $Ax = b$, and its slow convergence for large condition numbers motivates the conjugate gradient method and preconditioning.

blocks.body:
Picture standing on a hillside in fog, wanting to reach the valley floor. You cannot see the valley, but you can feel which way the ground slopes under your feet. A sensible strategy is to take a step downhill, feel again, and repeat. Gradient descent is this strategy for a function of many variables: the gradient points uphill most steeply, so we step the opposite way.

The questions are how long the steps should be, how fast the method converges, and what can go wrong. We use gradients from [[partial-derivatives]] and [[convexity]].

blocks.title: The method and the step size
blocks.body:
For a differentiable $f\colon \mathbb{R}^n \to \mathbb{R}$, the directional derivative in a unit direction $u$ is $\nabla f(x)\cdot u$, which by Cauchy-Schwarz is smallest when $u$ points along $-\nabla f(x)$. Gradient descent takes a step of size proportional to the gradient in that direction:
$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\,\nabla f(x_k),$$
where $\eta > 0$ is the step size (in machine learning, the learning rate). If $\nabla f(x_k) = 0$ the method stops moving, so its fixed points are exactly the critical points of $f$.

The step size matters a great deal. Take $f(x) = x^2$, so $f'(x) = 2x$ and $x_{k+1} = (1 - 2\eta)x_k$. The iterates go to the minimum $0$ exactly when $|1 - 2\eta| < 1$, that is $0 < \eta < 1$. With $\eta = 0.1$ the error shrinks by $0.8$ each step; with $\eta = 0.5$ we land on $0$ at once; with $\eta = 0.9$ the iterates jump from side to side, shrinking by $0.8$; with $\eta = 1.1$ they jump and grow by $1.2$ each step. A step that is too large overshoots the valley and climbs the opposite slope.

What limits the step is the curvature. Here $f'' = 2$ and the bound was $\eta < 2/f''$. In general, the right measure is the smoothness constant.

blocks.title: Smoothness and strong convexity
blocks.body:
A differentiable $f$ is $L$-smooth if its gradient is $L$-Lipschitz: $\|
abla f(x) - 
abla f(y)\| \le L\|x - y\|$ for all $x, y$. It is $\mu$-strongly convex ($\mu > 0$) if
$$f(y) \ge f(x) + 
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y - x) +  rac{\mu}{2}\|y - x\|^2 \quad	ext{for all } x, y.$$
For twice differentiable $f$ these say that every eigenvalue of the Hessian lies in $[-L, L]$, respectively in $[\mu, \infty)$. The ratio $\kappa = L/\mu$ is the condition number: how much the curvature varies with direction.

blocks.title: Descent lemma
blocks.body:
If $f$ is $L$-smooth then $f(y) \le f(x) + \nabla f(x)^{\mathsf T}(y - x) + \frac L2\|y - x\|^2$ for all $x, y$. In particular, one gradient step with $\eta = 1/L$ satisfies
$$f(x_{k+1}) \le f(x_k) - \frac{1}{2L}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2.$$

blocks.title: Proof
blocks.body:
Let $d = y - x$ and $\varphi(t) = f(x + td)$, so $\varphi'(t) = 
abla f(x + td)^{\mathsf T}d$. By the fundamental theorem of calculus,
$$f(y) - f(x) - 
abla f(x)^{\mathsf T}d = \int_0^1  ig(
abla f(x + td) - 
abla f(x) ig)^{\mathsf T}d\,dt \le \int_0^1 L t\|d\|\cdot\|d\|\,dt =  rac L2\|d\|^2,$$
using Cauchy-Schwarz and the Lipschitz bound. For the second claim put $x = x_k$, $d = - rac1L
abla f(x_k)$: the right side becomes $f(x_k) -  rac1L\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2 +  rac{1}{2L}\|
abla f(x_k)\|^2$.

blocks.title: Convergence of gradient descent
blocks.body:
Run gradient descent with $\eta = 1/L$ on an $L$-smooth function $f$.

1. If $f$ is bounded below by $f_{\inf}$, then for every $K \ge 1$, $\displaystyle\min_{0 \le k < K}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \le \frac{2L\,(f(x_0) - f_{\inf})}{K}$.
2. (Stated without proof.) If $f$ is convex with a minimiser $x^\star$, then $f(x_k) - f^\star \le \dfrac{L\|x_0 - x^\star\|^2}{2k}$.
3. If $f$ is $\mu$-strongly convex with minimiser $x^\star$, then $f(x_k) - f^\star \le \left(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\right)^k(f(x_0) - f^\star)$.

Here $f^\star = f(x^\star)$.

blocks.title: Proof of parts 1 and 3
blocks.body:
Part 1: summing the descent lemma over $k = 0, \dots, K-1$, the values telescope:
$$\frac{1}{2L}\sum_{k=0}^{K-1}\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2 \le f(x_0) - f(x_K) \le f(x_0) - f_{\inf}.$$
The smallest of the $K$ terms is at most their average, which gives the bound.

Part 3: first, strong convexity bounds the gap by the gradient. The right side of the strong convexity inequality is a quadratic in $y$, minimised at $y = x - \frac1\mu\nabla f(x)$ with value $f(x) - \frac{1}{2\mu}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2$. So for every $y$, and in particular $y = x^\star$,
$$f^\star \ge f(x) - \frac{1}{2\mu}\|\nabla f(x)\|^2, \qquad\text{i.e.}\qquad \|\nabla f(x)\|^2 \ge 2\mu\,(f(x) - f^\star).$$
Insert this into the descent lemma:
$$f(x_{k+1}) - f^\star \le f(x_k) - f^\star - \frac{\mu}{L}(f(x_k) - f^\star) = \left(1 - \frac{\mu}{L}\right)(f(x_k) - f^\star),$$
and iterate. We do not prove part 2; its proof tracks $\|x_k - x^\star\|$ and is in Nesterov's book.

blocks.title: Why badly scaled problems are slow
blocks.body:
Part 1 is a guarantee even without convexity: gradient descent finds points where the gradient is small, at rate $1/K$, though such points may be saddle points or local minima. Part 3 is linear convergence: the number of steps to reach accuracy $\varepsilon$ grows like $\kappa\log(1/\varepsilon)$. So the condition number, not the dimension, governs the speed.

The picture behind this is a long, narrow valley. For $f(x, y) = \frac12(x^2 + 10y^2)$ the level curves are ellipses ten times more curved across ($y$) than along ($x$). The gradient $(x, 10y)$ points mostly across the valley, not along it toward the minimum. A step large enough to make progress along the valley overshoots across it, so the iterates zigzag, and a step small enough to avoid this crawls along the valley. Rescaling the variables to make the level sets round (preconditioning) removes the problem; Newton's method does this automatically by using the Hessian.

Momentum methods help too. The heavy-ball method adds a fraction of the previous step, $x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta\nabla f(x_k) + \beta(x_k - x_{k-1})$, which damps the zigzag and builds up speed along the valley. Nesterov's accelerated method improves the rates to $O(1/k^2)$ in part 2 and to roughly $1 - 1/\sqrt{\kappa}$ per step in part 3, and these rates are the best possible for methods that use only gradients, in a precise sense (results we quote without proof).

blocks.title: Stochastic gradient descent
blocks.body:
In statistics and machine learning the function is usually an average over data: $f(x) =  rac1N\sum_{i=1}^N f_i(x)$, where $f_i$ measures how badly the model with parameters $x$ fits data point $i$. With $N$ in the millions, even one full gradient is expensive. Stochastic gradient descent (SGD) picks a random index $i_k$ and uses only that term:
$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \eta_k\,
abla f_{i_k}(x_k).$$
If $i_k$ is uniform, the expected value of $
abla f_{i_k}(x)$ is exactly $
abla f(x)$: the step is right on average, at $1/N$ of the cost. In practice one uses a mini-batch, the average gradient over a small random set of indices, which reduces the noise.

The noise does not vanish at the minimum, because individual $
abla f_i(x^\star)$ are not zero. With a fixed step, SGD therefore approaches the minimum and then jitters around it in a region whose size is proportional to $\eta$. To converge one lets $\eta_k$ decrease, classically with $\sum_k \eta_k = \infty$ and $\sum_k \eta_k^2 < \infty$ (for example $\eta_k = c/(k+1)$), the conditions of Robbins and Monro (1951). Popular variants such as Adam adapt the step size separately for each coordinate. For neural networks the gradients $
abla f_i$ are computed by backpropagation, which is the chain rule organised efficiently.

blocks.title: Example 1: zigzag in a narrow valley
blocks.body: Apply gradient descent to $f(x, y) = \frac12(x^2 + 10y^2)$ from $(10, 1)$ with $\eta = \frac{2}{11}$, and then with $\eta = \frac{1}{10}$. Compare with the bound of part 3.
blocks.solution:
The gradient is $(x, 10y)$, so a step maps $(x, y)$ to $\big((1 - \eta)x,\ (1 - 10\eta)y\big)$. Here $\mu = 1$, $L = 10$, $f^\star = 0$ and $f(10, 1) = 55$.

With $\eta = \frac2{11}$ the factors are $\frac{9}{11}$ and $1 - \frac{20}{11} = -\frac{9}{11}$, so
$$(x_k, y_k) = \left(10\left(\tfrac{9}{11}\right)^k,\ \left(-\tfrac{9}{11}\right)^k\right), \qquad f(x_k, y_k) = 55\left(\tfrac{9}{11}\right)^{2k}.$$
The sign of $y$ flips every step: the iterates zigzag across the valley. The value shrinks by $\left(\frac{9}{11}\right)^2 \approx 0.669$ per step.

With $\eta = \frac1{10} = \frac1L$ the factors are $0.9$ and $0$: the $y$-coordinate is fixed in one step, and then $x$ shrinks by $0.9$ per step, so $f(x_k, y_k) = 50\cdot 0.81^k$ for $k \ge 1$. Part 3 promises $f(x_k) \le 55\cdot 0.9^k$, and indeed $50\cdot 0.81^k \le 55\cdot 0.9^k$. To get $f$ below $10^{-6}$ takes $k = 85$ steps with $\eta = \frac{1}{10}$; the condition number $\kappa = 10$ is what makes it take so long, compared with one step for the round bowl $\frac12(x^2 + y^2)$.

blocks.title: Example 2: the best constant step for a quadratic
blocks.body: For $f(x) = \frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Ax$ with $A$ symmetric and eigenvalues in $[\mu, L]$, $0 < \mu < L$, gradient descent gives $x_{k+1} = (I - \eta A)x_k$. Which $\eta$ minimises the worst-case contraction factor $\max_{\lambda\in[\mu, L]}|1 - \eta\lambda|$, and what is the optimal factor?
blocks.solution:
In the eigenbasis of $A$ each coordinate is multiplied by $1 - \eta\lambda_i$, so the error contracts by $\max_i|1 - \eta\lambda_i|$ per step in the worst case. The function $\lambda \mapsto |1 - \eta\lambda|$ is convex and piecewise linear, so its maximum over $[\mu, L]$ is at an endpoint: $\rho(\eta) = \max(|1 - \eta\mu|, |1 - \eta L|)$.

As $\eta$ grows, $|1 - \eta\mu|$ decreases (while $\eta < 1/\mu$) and $|1 - \eta L|$ eventually increases, so the best $\eta$ balances them: $1 - \eta\mu = \eta L - 1$, giving
$$\eta^\star = \frac{2}{L + \mu}, \qquad \rho^\star = \frac{L - \mu}{L + \mu} = \frac{\kappa - 1}{\kappa + 1}.$$
For any other $\eta$ one of the two endpoint values is larger. In Example 1, $\mu = 1$, $L = 10$ gives $\eta^\star = \frac{2}{11}$ and $\rho^\star = \frac{9}{11}$, exactly the factors we saw. Convergence happens for every $\eta \in (0, 2/L)$, since then both endpoint values are below $1$. When $\kappa$ is large, $\rho^\star \approx 1 - 2/\kappa$, so the number of steps needed is proportional to $\kappa$.

blocks.title: Example 3: SGD computes a running average
blocks.body: Take the made-up data set $a = (2, 4, 4, 5, 7, 8)$ and $f(x) = \frac1{6}\sum_i \frac12(x - a_i)^2$, minimised at the mean $5$. Run SGD with $\eta_k = \frac{1}{k+1}$, $k = 0, 1, 2, \dots$, sampling one data point per step. What does $x_k$ equal? What happens with a fixed step $\eta = 0.1$?
blocks.solution:
Here $\nabla f_i(x) = x - a_i$. Write $b_k = a_{i_k}$ for the sampled value. The first step gives $x_1 = x_0 - (x_0 - b_0) = b_0$, whatever $x_0$ was. Then
$$x_{k+1} = x_k - \frac{1}{k+1}(x_k - b_k) = \frac{k\,x_k + b_k}{k+1}.$$
If $x_k = \frac1k(b_0 + \cdots + b_{k-1})$, this gives $x_{k+1} = \frac{1}{k+1}(b_0 + \cdots + b_k)$. So by induction $x_k$ is exactly the average of the first $k$ samples. By the law of large numbers ([[limit-theorems]]) it converges to the mean $5$, with standard deviation $\sigma/\sqrt k$, where $\sigma^2 = 4$ is the variance of the data.

With a fixed step, $x_{k+1} = 0.9\,x_k + 0.1\,b_k$, an exponentially weighted average of recent samples. It never settles. In the long run its variance $v$ satisfies $v = 0.81v + 0.01\sigma^2$, so $v = \frac{0.01\cdot 4}{0.19} = \frac{4}{19} \approx 0.21$, a standard deviation of about $0.46$ around the mean. A smaller fixed step shrinks this jitter but slows the approach; decreasing steps get both.

blocks.body:
- Gradient descent finds critical points, not global minima. On a nonconvex function it may stop at a local minimum, and if started exactly at a saddle or a maximum it stays there. The convergence rates in parts 2 and 3 need convexity.
- The step bound $\eta < 2/L$ is about the largest curvature. A step that works in one region can diverge in a steeper one, which is why practical codes use line searches or step-size schedules.
- A small gradient does not imply being close to the minimiser when the function is very flat: for $f(x) = x^4$ the gradient near $0$ is tiny long before $x$ is.
- Gradient descent is not invariant under rescaling variables. Measuring one variable in millimetres instead of metres changes the condition number and the speed; Newton's method does not have this problem.
- With SGD, a fixed learning rate cannot give exact convergence; plateaus of the training loss often just reflect the noise level set by $\eta$.

Gradient descent is the basic algorithm of [[convex-optimisation]], where the KKT theory tells us when the critical point it finds is optimal; projected gradient descent handles constraints by projecting each step back onto the feasible set. For the quadratic $\frac12 x^{\mathsf T}Ax - b^{\mathsf T}x$ it is an iterative solver for linear systems, related to [[least-squares]] and to the eigenvalues of [[spectral-theorem|symmetric matrices]]. Viewed with $\eta \to 0$ it becomes the gradient flow $x' = -\nabla f(x)$, and the method itself is Euler's method for this differential equation (see [[numerical-odes]]). Its fixed-point analysis is an instance of the [[contraction-mapping]] principle, and the one-dimensional analogue for solving equations is in [[root-finding]]. SGD's noise analysis connects to [[martingales]] and stochastic approximation.

1. For $f(x,y) = x^2 + xy + y^2$, find $L$ and $\mu$, and the step size that makes gradient descent contract fastest.
2. Show that if $f$ is $L$-smooth and $\eta \in (0, 2/L)$, then $f(x_{k+1}) \le f(x_k) - \eta\left(1 - \frac{L\eta}{2}\right)\|\nabla f(x_k)\|^2$.
3. Run three steps of gradient descent with $\eta = 0.1$ on $f(x) = x^4 - 2x^2$ starting from $x_0 = 0.5$. Which critical point do the iterates approach?
4. In Example 3, show that with fixed step $\eta \in (0, 2)$ the long-run variance is $\frac{\eta\,\sigma^2}{2 - \eta}$.
